notes.meaning: God gave this prophetic message to Jeremiah near the start of King Zedekiah's rule over Judah. Even though Zedekiah belonged to the royal line of godly King Josiah, his reign faced immediate crisis. Jeremiah was tasked with delivering a hard truth from the Lord to the new king and surrounding nations.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars note that older Hebrew manuscripts read Jehoiakim here, which likely entered the text as an early scribal copying error since the rest of the chapter clearly addresses King Zedekiah around 594 BC.

notes.meaning: God told Jeremiah to make a wooden farm yoke held together by leather straps and wear it on his own neck. Foreign ambassadors from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon had arrived in Jerusalem to plan a joint revolt against Babylon. Jeremiah was commanded to send yokes to their rulers as a physical sign that God had already placed them under Babylonian authority.

Jeremiah was instructed to deliver a message directly to these foreign kings from the Lord of Hosts, the God of Israel. God reminded them that He alone created the entire earth, along with every person and beast living on it. Because He is the Creator and rightful owner of the world, He has the authority to hand earthly rule to whomever He pleases.

God announced that He had chosen King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon to govern all these territories. God called this pagan ruler His servant because Nebuchadnezzar was an instrument carrying out God's sovereign plans, not because he was a worshiper of the true God. The Lord even subjected the wild animals to him to show how absolute his dominion would be.

The neighboring countries were told that they would serve Nebuchadnezzar, his son Evil-merodach, and his grandson Belshazzar. Babylon's empire would not last forever, but would run until its appointed time arrived. When that seventy-year period ended, God would bring other powerful nations to conquer and enslave Babylon.

Any nation that refused to bow to Nebuchadnezzar and accept his yoke would face severe punishment from the Lord. God warned that war, starvation, and deadly plague would destroy anyone who resisted. Fighting against Babylon was useless because it was rebellion against God's direct decree.

The rulers were told to stop listening to their fortune-tellers, dream interpreters, mediums, and sorcerers. These pagan advisors claimed to predict the future and promised that Babylon would never conquer them. In truth, their flattering lies would only trick the leaders into fighting, leading to total defeat and banishment from their land.

God promised that any kingdom willing to submit peacefully to the king of Babylon would be allowed to stay home. They would have to pay taxes to Nebuchadnezzar, but they could cultivate their fields and live in peace. Humbly accepting God's discipline always shields people from greater disaster.

Jeremiah took the very same warning straight to Zedekiah, the king of Judah. He pleaded with the king to put his neck under Babylon's yoke so that he and his citizens could live. Resisting Babylon would only bring unnecessary death to Jerusalem through invasion, famine, and sickness.

King Zedekiah was warned to turn away from the local prophets in Jerusalem who urged him to rebel against Babylon. The Lord had never sent these men, yet they were speaking falsehoods while claiming to speak for God. Listening to their fake promises would bring divine judgment and ruin on the king and the prophets alike.

Jeremiah went to the temple to warn the priests and all the worshippers. Popular voices were reassuring the people that the holy temple items taken during earlier raids would very soon be returned from Babylon. Jeremiah declared that this hope was false and urged them to serve Babylon instead so the holy city would not become a wasteland.

Jeremiah challenged these rival prophets to prove their calling by their prayers. A true prophet's duty was to plead with the Lord to protect the people and turn away judgment. If they really had God's ear, they should have been praying that the remaining treasures in the temple and the royal palace would not be carried off as well.

The Lord spoke specifically about the heavy bronze furnishings still standing in the temple, such as the two great bronze pillars, the giant water basin called the sea, and the movable stands. Nebuchadnezzar had left these behind when he exiled King Jehoiachin and Judah's noble leaders. God warned that these remaining treasures in the temple and city were about to meet the same fate.

God warned that every remaining sacred vessel would be taken to Babylon until He decided to intervene. He closed with a gracious promise that their stay would not be permanent. When God's appointed time of seventy years arrived, He would restore those sacred treasures back to their proper place in Jerusalem.
